turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Come through and take a seat. The highway looked nasty — was the traffic bad on your way in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. It was rather slow past the servo, but I allowed extra time, so I was not late.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good on you. Reception has you down for a repeat-script review, and they said you wanted a word about the pain tablets as well.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): That is correct. I would be grateful if we could review the regular medicines and, if you thought it appropriate, something a little stronger for the knees.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. In your own words, how are the knees behaving?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Both of them ache, the right more than the left. It is a dull pain, moderate I would say, and it has been present for five-ish years. Stairs and the walk to the shops are the worst of it.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five-ish years, both knees. What takes the edge off, if anything?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Rest helps, and the paracetamol does take the edge off, though it never truly settles, particularly in the evenings. I take paracetamol five hundred milligrams, two tablets, four times a day.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the anti-inflammatory — still on that?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Meloxicam, fifteen milligrams, once each morning with breakfast. I have been on it for about two years, for the osteoarthritis.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any heartburn with it, or black stools?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No heartburn, and no black stools. I am quite careful to take it with food.

[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. The pharmacy technician printed the chemist list this morning, so I'll read it and you tell me if it matches. Atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night, ramipril five milligrams in the morning, plus the paracetamol and the meloxicam as you've just said.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The ramipril five milligrams each morning is correct. The atorvastatin, however, is not — I take forty milligrams at night. Well, actually, the packet at home plainly says forty. My previous doctor increased it, though I cannot recall the month.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hmm. Twenty on the pharmacy list, forty on your packet. I'm not going to pick a winner without seeing the box, so the dose stays unsettled for today.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I do apologise for the confusion. I also, um, miss the occasional night with it, if I am being honest. Perhaps two nights a week.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's worth knowing, and it muddies things further. Bring the box next time and we'll reconcile it properly. I won't issue a statin script today.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course. I shall bring it.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Now, the stronger painkiller. You were hoping for something more than the paracetamol and the meloxicam.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. I wondered whether tramadol might be suitable. A friend mentioned oxycodone, but I would not wish to be presumptuous. I simply find the evenings difficult.

[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think this through out loud. Full-dose paracetamol, daily meloxicam, longstanding osteoarthritis. I could start tramadol fifty milligrams twice a day — sorry, no, fifty milligrams at night to start, not twice. That was my first thought.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): If you felt that was suitable, I would be most grateful.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Before I commit to that, any dizziness? Any falls?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): There was one turn of dizziness last month. I nearly fell in the kitchen. It passed within a few minutes, and it has not come back.

[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah, that changes it. Tramadol, or oxycodone for that matter, would be a poor idea after a near-fall, especially with the ramipril on board. I'm not prescribing either. Scratch the tramadol.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand completely. I would rather be safe.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): I had also been going to order a kidney blood test today, what with the meloxicam and the ramipril together.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I had blood tests at the public hospital about three weeks ago. They told me the kidneys were all right. The letter is at home with the statin box.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I won't order bloods today. If that letter doesn't actually show a kidney result, we'll do the test when you come back. No point sticking you twice.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): That seems very sensible. Thank you.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): While I write the other scripts — paracetamol, meloxicam and the ramipril, same doses you've confirmed — how was the rest of the drive, apart from the servo?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, the highway was crawling. A cricket match was letting out at the oval, the under-fourteens, and the cars were banked up for ages.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is your grandson still in that side?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, young Thomas. He bowled four overs on Saturday and was terribly pleased with himself. They lost, mind you, but he took a wicket with a slower ball, or so he tells me.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): A slower ball at that age, good on him. The weather held for you, at least. It bucketed down here on Friday arvo.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): We were lucky. His mother packed oranges and he ate the lot. He has asked for new white boots for his birthday, which I fear will be filthy within a week.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): They always are. Right — back to the scripts, before I lose my place.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): There is one other thing, if I may. There is a little morning stiffness, perhaps ten minutes, and then it loosens.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ten minutes is more the wear-and-tear pattern than an inflammatory one. I think this is osteoarthritis of the knees, the same diagnosis you've carried. I'm not calling it anything new.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that is what I was told. I have no swelling that I can see, if that is of any relevance. I do apologise for not mentioning the stiffness earlier.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): No harm done. Let me just feel the right knee. No warmth, and no fluid in the joint. There is crepitus when you bend it, and the left one is quieter.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): It does click, yes. Is there anything I ought to do differently at home?

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the paracetamol regular, not only when the pain is bad — two tablets, four times a day, as you are already doing. Do not add ibuprofen, or any other anti-inflammatory, on top of the meloxicam. A warm pack in the evening is perfectly reasonable.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall do that. I do not take ibuprofen.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in four weeks with the statin box and the hospital letter. If the pain becomes severe before then, come back sooner and we'll rethink, still without jumping to an opioid.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate you explaining it so carefully, and I shall see you in four weeks.

spec.situation: Routine repeat-prescription review at a small clinic with a pharmacy technician present; patient wants a stronger painkiller; tablet names and doses are discussed in detail, one dose is read from the pharmacy list and differs from the patient's own; doctor declines the stronger medicine.
features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

bad.reason: Clicking is supported, but transcript doesn't specify right knee; doctor notes right knee crepitus.
bad.text: knee clicking (category=musculoskeletal, status=present, temporality=current, body_site=right knee, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Patient reported the recent hospital blood tests were done about three weeks ago and that they were told the kidneys were all right.
Doctor explicitly said they would not order bloods today because recent hospital tests may already include kidney results.
Doctor initially considered tramadol and corrected themself: first thought was tramadol 50 mg at night to start, not twice a day, before ultimately deciding not to prescribe it.
Doctor noted the left knee was quieter on examination.
